description: VeriVul is a dataset of 13,908 formally verified, self-contained programs (10,225 vulnerable, 3,683 safe; C, C++ and Python) that a pipeline of LLMs generated from real CVE seed functions of ReposVul and ICVul. Every program carries an ESBMC 8.4 k-induction verdict (a counterexample with the violating statement, or a proof), and C and C++ programs carry an AddressSanitizer/UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer record: the reproducing input for vulnerable programs and the bounded search outcome for safe programs. 102 vulnerable/safe pairs share a seed lineage. The release also contains the evaluation sets, model predictions, realism and memorisation analyses of the accompanying paper, and the framework that generates and verifies the programs.
citeAs: Lekssays, A., Mouhcine, H., Khalil, I. VeriVul: A Verification-Guided Framework for Generating Realistic Vulnerability Benchmarks. NeurIPS 2026 Evaluations and Datasets Track.
rai:dataLimitations: Labels describe programs under ESBMC's model, not the source CVE. Known limits inherited from ESBMC 8.4: (1) a SAFE verdict requires that every loop is unrolled within the time budget (290, 590 or 1,790 s), so programs with large input-dependent bounds are absent and the data is biased towards moderate size (median 163 lines, maximum 1,860); (2) calls such as stat, open, localtime and rand return unconstrained values, so some violations depend on results a real system never returns (flag env_dependent, 2,972 programs); (3) unprovided command-line arguments are NULL, so programs read no arguments; (4) library models can differ from the real functions (a strstr model with an embedded NUL byte proves a crashing program safe); (5) unsigned wraparound and misaligned accesses are not checked, and uninitialised reads, format strings and data races are not checked in this configuration. The bounded sanitizer search found a failing input for 42 of 3,626 SAFE C/C++ programs (13 of 3,442 C, 29 of 184 C++; flag sanitizer_counterexample_on_safe); 258 programs have an empty main (flag empty_main; a SAFE verdict on them is vacuous). The programs are C/C++-heavy (87.4% C, 12.2% C++, 0.4% Python, all Python programs SAFE and without sanitizer checks), cover memory-safety and arithmetic weaknesses (123 target CWEs, top five CWE-125, 787, 190, 476, 416), and only 102 vulnerable/safe pairs are verified minimal edits. Programs written by gpt-oss-120b (52% of the vulnerable programs) are farther from real-world code than those of the other generators (Appendix K of the paper). Not recommended for: certifying that a program is free of vulnerabilities, measuring detection of weaknesses outside the checked classes, training or evaluating detectors for other languages or for logic and concurrency bugs, or any claim that a label matches the CVE of its seed.
rai:dataBiases: Selection bias: seeds come from ReposVul and ICVul (open-source C/C++ projects with public CVE fixes; 440 projects, 1,430 CVEs, Linux kernel and a few large projects dominate), so the data over-represents widely used open-source projects and memory-safety CWEs. Verifier bias: only programs that ESBMC verifies within budget enter the dataset, which removes large, loop-heavy and environment-heavy programs. Generator bias: five LLMs wrote the programs (gpt-oss-120b 40.5%, gemma-4-31b-it 28.9%, seed-coder-8b 22.0%, qwen3.6-35b-a3b 5.8%, qwen3.8-27b 2.7%) and their style and CWE mix differ; the generation prompts ask for production-style code without security-suggestive comments, which shapes the code. Label bias: SAFE programs are safe only for the checked properties; vulnerable programs describe the defect ESBMC found, which can differ from the defect of the seed (sanitizer agreement: 31.3% exact line and class, 4.6% function and class, 45.3% class only, 18.8% a different defect). Models can over-flag programs as vulnerable (recall 83-97%, precision 52-66% in our evaluation).
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: None intended. The programs are LLM-generated code. Records carry the public CVE identifier, project name, repository URL and commit hash of the seed. Commit messages and author fields of the source corpora are not included. Some generated programs contain placeholder strings such as user@EXAMPLE.COM or 127.0.0.1; these are not personal data. No demographic, health, political or religious information is present.
rai:dataUseCases: Validated: (a) benchmarking LLMs and detectors on whole-program vulnerability detection with formally derived labels and trigger lines (Section 5.2 of the paper); (b) root-cause localisation against the ESBMC counterexample; (c) studying verifier-grounded synthetic data generation and its realism (Section 5.1); (d) contamination-resilient evaluation, since the programs were generated after the training cutoff of the probed models (memorisation probe, Appendix L). Plausible but not validated: fine-tuning or reinforcement learning with verified labels; evaluation of other verifiers or sanitizers. Not validated: measuring real-world exploitability, evaluating detectors on other CWE classes or languages. Use the strict subset (data/subsets/ids_strict.txt) to exclude flagged programs.
rai:dataSocialImpact: Positive: more accurate evaluation of vulnerability detectors, reduced reliance on noisy commit-derived labels, and a regenerable resource that limits benchmark contamination. Negative: vulnerable programs and their reproducing inputs could help attackers study memory-safety bugs. Mitigations: the programs are small self-contained programs that crash a local binary, not exploits against deployed systems, they target publicly disclosed and fixed CVE classes, and the inputs trigger sanitizer reports rather than weaponised payloads. A detector trained on the data can over-flag or miss vulnerabilities outside the checked classes, so it should not be the sole basis for security decisions.

prov:wasGeneratedBy.description: ESBMC 8.4 (docker image digest in each record) with k-induction, a 64-bit memory model, main as entry point, and the flags recorded in verification.command. Programs with a timeout, memory exhaustion or frontend error are discarded.

SAFE programs are re-searched with the same seeded search (40 s).

rai:dataCollection: Synthetic generation from real CVE seeds; no human data collection. Seeds: ReposVul and ICVul pre-fix functions. Programs generated in October 2026 on a self-hosted GPU deployment with the framework in framework/.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Programs are used as generated. Programs that do not compile or that ESBMC cannot decide are discarded. No two released programs have the same text (checked by SHA-256). Flags mark programs with a sanitizer counterexample on a SAFE label, an empty main, a lexically obvious vulnerability, or an environment-dependent verdict; flagged programs are kept and listed in data/subsets.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Labels are produced mechanically, not by annotators. A SAFE label states that ESBMC proves that none of the checked properties is violated on any execution of the program. The proof holds under the configuration in verification.command and its modelling assumptions: allocation never fails, execution is sequential, input from standard input, files and the environment is arbitrary, and library functions follow ESBMC's operational models. A VULNERABLE label states that ESBMC found an execution that violates a checked property. Both labels describe the program, not the source CVE: they do not certify that a program contains the defect of its seed. For C and C++ the verdict is complemented by a sanitizer check: a VULNERABLE program must fail under AddressSanitizer or UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer on some input (stored with the record), and a SAFE program must survive a bounded input search. The search is bounded, so it adds evidence to the verdict and does not prove it.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: Static release, version 1.0.0, on Zenodo (DOI assigned on publication). The pipeline can regenerate new snapshots from fresh CVEs; new snapshots will be released as new versions of the record with a changelog. Issues are tracked in the framework repository.
